client: I'm just so anxious about this big presentation I have to give next week. I totally blanked on my lines during practice yesterday, and now I can't stop worrying that it'll happen again in front of everyone. Part of me feels like talking about it won't really help because the damage is already done - I know I'm going to mess up.
therapist: It sounds like this presentation has been weighing heavily on you, and that moment of blanking during practice really shook your confidence. I’m curious—when those thoughts come up about messing up again, how do they affect the way you’re preparing now?

client: Honestly, those thoughts make it hard to focus when I’m preparing. I keep getting distracted by imagining the worst-case scenarios—people laughing at me or thinking I’m incompetent. I know I should be practicing more, but it feels pointless because I’m already convinced I’ll fail.
therapist: It's understandable that those vivid worst-case scenarios would make it so difficult to focus—our minds have a way of making imagined failures feel very real and threatening. I wonder if we could explore together what might happen if you tried redirecting your attention to just one small, manageable part of the presentation for now?

client: I guess I could try focusing on just one part, but I’m not sure it’ll help because the whole thing feels overwhelming. What if I get stuck on that one part too? It’s hard to shake the feeling that I’m just not good at this, no matter how much I try to break it down.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming this feels—like no amount of breaking it down can shift that core belief about not being good at this. What’s something small you’ve succeeded at in the past, even if it felt insignificant at the time?

client: Hmm, I guess I did okay on a smaller project last month—nothing big, but I got positive feedback. Still, it feels different because that wasn’t in front of a group or under so much pressure. I’m not sure how that helps me now—this feels like a completely different level of stress.
therapist: It’s true that this situation feels different with higher stakes, but I notice you’re discounting that past success as irrelevant—could we explore what skills or strengths helped you succeed then that might still apply here?

client: I did prepare carefully for that last project, and I was pretty organized about it. But with this presentation, my mind just goes blank when I think about people watching me—I don’t think preparation helps when my anxiety takes over like that. It’s like my brain short-circuits in front of an audience no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like your anxiety in front of an audience feels like it overrides all the preparation you’ve done, which must be incredibly frustrating. I wonder if we could explore ways to practice managing that anxiety in smaller, low-stakes situations to help build your confidence?

client: I guess practicing in smaller situations might help, but it’s hard to imagine anything feeling “low-stakes” when it comes to public speaking. Even just the idea of practicing in front of a friend makes me nervous—I feel like I’ll still freeze up, and then I’ll just feel embarrassed. What if I can’t even handle that?
therapist: It’s clear how much pressure you’re putting on yourself, even in smaller situations—that fear of freezing up and feeling embarrassed is really intense. What would it feel like to let yourself take one tiny step, like practicing in front of a friend with the understanding that it’s okay to stumble a bit?

client: I don't know... even the idea of stumbling in front of a friend makes me feel like a failure. What if they think less of me afterwards? I keep imagining their awkward pity or them thinking "wow, she really can't handle this." It's like any mistake confirms all my worst fears about myself.
therapist: It sounds like your fear of judgment, even from someone supportive, is deeply tied to how you see yourself—like any mistake feels like proof of inadequacy. I wonder if we could explore how you’d respond if a friend stumbled during a presentation—would you judge them as harshly as you’re judging yourself?

client: That's... actually a good point. If my friend messed up, I'd probably feel bad for them but I wouldn't think they were incompetent. So why do I think that way about myself? It's just hard to believe others would be that understanding toward me. I always assume people are noticing and judging every mistake.
therapist: It’s interesting how much more compassion you’re able to extend to others than to yourself—it sounds like you hold yourself to a much stricter standard. What might it feel like to experiment with treating yourself with the same kindness you’d offer a friend?

client: I get what you're saying, but it feels different when it's about me. Like I should know better or be better prepared. Even the idea of being kind to myself about mistakes feels like making excuses for not being good enough. It's like I'd be letting myself off the hook when I should be pushing harder.
therapist: I hear how deeply you believe that pushing yourself harder is the only way to succeed, and that being kind to yourself feels like giving up or making excuses. I wonder if we could explore what it might feel like to balance kindness with preparation—could those two things coexist?

client: I don’t know—it feels like kindness and preparation are opposites. If I’m kind to myself, I’ll slack off, and if I push myself, I’ll do better. But honestly, pushing myself hasn’t worked so far—it just makes me more anxious. Maybe there’s some middle ground, but I’m not sure how to find it without feeling like I’m just being lazy or avoiding the hard work.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between two extremes—kindness feels like slacking off, and pushing yourself feels like it’s only making things worse. I wonder if we could explore what a balanced approach might look like—one that includes both preparation and self-compassion, without the fear of letting yourself down?
